questions.statement: Complete the sentence: My birthday is ... March.
questions.context: Maria is planning her exam calendar for the spring term in Valencia.

options.feedback: In is correct because English uses in with months, seasons and years, so in March names the month of the birthday.
On is wrong here because on is reserved for days and full dates, like on Monday or on 5 May.
At is wrong because at works with clock times and fixed points, such as at noon, not with whole months.
By is wrong because by expresses a deadline, meaning not later than a moment, and the sentence needs the month itself.

questions.explanation:
Months always take the preposition in. English also uses in with years and seasons, while on goes with days and at with clock times.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: The English exam is ... Monday.
questions.context: The exchange students from Seville settle into their new school timetable.

options.feedback: In is wrong because in covers months, years and seasons, never a named day of the week.
On is correct because days of the week and dates take on, and Monday morning is still a day expression.
At is wrong because at points to exact clock times like at eight, so it cannot introduce a weekday.
Since is wrong because since marks a starting point in the past, as in since 2020, not a future day.

questions.explanation:
We say on Monday, on Friday morning and on 3 May. In would fit a month or a year, and at fits a clock time.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: Classes begin ... half past eight.
questions.context: The school day in Madrid starts earlier than many visitors expect.

options.feedback: On is wrong because on goes with days and dates, and half past eight is a time of day, not a date.
In is wrong because in suits longer periods such as months or the morning, not one exact clock reading.
At is correct because exact clock times always take at, so at half past eight is the natural form.
For is wrong because for measures duration, as in for two hours, and cannot place a single moment.

questions.explanation:
Clock times take at: at three, at noon, at half past eight. Days take on and longer periods take in.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: The first contest took place ... 2021.
questions.context: A bilingual school in Zaragoza celebrates the anniversary of its debate contest.

options.feedback: On is wrong because on needs a day or a full date, and a year on its own never takes it.
At is wrong because at attaches to clock times and points like at Christmas, not to a whole year.
From is wrong because from states a starting point and needs its partner to, as in from 2021 to 2025.
In is correct because bare years take in, so in 2021 is the standard way to place an event in a year.

questions.explanation:
Years, months and seasons form the group that takes in. On needs a day, and at needs a clock time or point.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: The final exam is ... 12 June.
questions.context: A student copies the exam timetable from the noticeboard for her classmates.

options.feedback: On is correct because a full date with a day number always takes on, so on 12 June is right.
In is wrong because in fits the month alone, as in in June, but the sentence names one exact day.
At is wrong because at belongs to clock times, and 12 June is a calendar date, not a time.
During is wrong because during means inside a period, as in during June, without fixing one day.

questions.explanation:
Specific dates take on: on 12 June, on 1 May. The preposition in appears only with the month or year alone.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: I will wait for you ... the bus stop.
questions.context: Two friends agree where to meet before the library opens.

options.feedback: In is wrong because in would mean inside a larger space, like in the station, and a bus stop is a point.
At is correct because at marks an exact meeting point, and a bus stop is precisely that kind of place.
On is wrong because on needs a surface or a line, as in on the corner, and the stop itself is a point.
To is wrong because to shows direction of movement, as in go to, but nobody is moving in this sentence.

questions.explanation:
Use at for a specific point: at the bus stop, at the door, at the crossroads. In suggests inside a space.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: The dinosaur skeletons are ... the main hall.
questions.context: The class visits the science museum in Bilbao on a rainy morning.

options.feedback: At is wrong because at treats the hall as a bare location point and loses the inside meaning.
On is wrong because on demands contact with a surface, like on the floor, and this is about the room.
In is correct because the skeletons stand inside the hall, and in expresses that enclosed position.
Over is wrong because over means above without touching, as in over the table, not inside a space.

questions.explanation:
Enclosed spaces take in: in the hall, in the box, in the room. At only points to the place as a dot on a map.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: Your notebook is ... the desk.
questions.context: A tidy student keeps her study notes where she can see them at home.

options.feedback: In is wrong because in means inside something, like in the drawer, and that is a different place.
At is wrong because at gives a general location, as in at the desk, without the contact with the surface.
Under is wrong because under means directly below, so the notebook would be hidden from sight.
On is correct because the notebook rests in contact with the surface of the desk, which is what on means.

questions.explanation:
Surfaces take on: on the desk, on the wall, on the shelf. In means inside, and under means below something.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: The train leaves ... 7.45 in the morning.
questions.context: A weekend plan described to a friend who asks for the exact hour.

options.feedback: At is correct because at introduces a precise clock time, and 7.45 is an exact hour.
In is wrong because in belongs to parts of the day such as in the morning, not to a number.
On is wrong because on marks days and dates, as in on Monday, and no day appears here.
By is wrong because by means no later than, which states a deadline instead of a departure time.

questions.explanation:
Clock times always take at: at 7.45, at midnight. Use in with parts of the day and on with days and dates.

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: They have been in Seville ... August.
questions.context: A student describing a holiday that began in the past and is still going on.

options.feedback: For is wrong because for measures the length of the stay, and the sentence names the starting month.
Since is correct because since names the starting point of a period that continues now.
During is wrong because during introduces a finished interval, while the stay has not ended.
At is wrong because at marks points and clock times, never the beginning of a lasting situation.

questions.explanation:
Since names the origin of an unfinished period, so they have been in Seville since August. For would give the duration instead.

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: The Prado museum is ... the Retiro park.
questions.context: A map exercise about where a famous museum stands in relation to a park.

options.feedback: Between needs three referents, as in between A and B, so it needs another landmark in this sentence.
Above describes a vertical position and says nothing about being close on the same level.
Next to is correct because next to expresses adjacency between two neighbouring places.
During belongs to time and cannot describe the position of a building on a map.

questions.explanation:
Next to states that two places touch. Between always requires two names around the preposition, so it does not fit here.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence where every preposition is correct.
questions.context: A sentence to be repaired because the preposition does not fit the meaning.

options.text: The shop opens in nine and closes on seven in the evening.
options.feedback: In does not combine with a number such as nine when naming an opening hour.

options.text: The shop opens on nine and closes at seven in the evening.
options.feedback: On marks days and dates, so it cannot introduce the hour at which the shop opens.

options.text: The shop opens on nine and closes on seven in the evening.
options.feedback: Using on for both hours gives the sentence two prepositions that belong to a different category.

options.text: The shop opens at nine and closes at seven in the evening.
options.feedback: Both times take at, which is the preposition English reserves for clock times.

questions.explanation:
The hour of opening and closing is a clock time in both halves of the sentence, and clock times always take at.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: She put her coat ... the empty chair beside her.
questions.context: A child asking a teacher for permission during a school trip.

options.feedback: On is correct because the coat rests on a surface, and the chair seat provides that surface.
In needs a container or an enclosed space, and a chair is neither of them.
At would give a general location without the contact that a coat on a chair implies.
Between needs two objects with the preposition in the middle, and only one object is named here.

questions.explanation:
Clothes placed on furniture take on: on the chair, on the bed, on the sofa. In would require a bag or a wardrobe.

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: The school trip to the science museum takes place ... May.
questions.context: A teenager talking about an event that happens once every year.

options.feedback: At belongs to points and clock times and cannot introduce a month.
In is correct because in introduces a month, and May appears without a day number.
On would need a full date, as in on 5 May, but no day is given in the sentence.
To indicates direction or a recipient and does not place an event inside a month.

questions.explanation:
A month on its own takes in: in May, in winter. On appears only when a specific day is attached, as in on 5 May.

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: I left the keys ... the small table near the door.
questions.context: A worker describing where the keys ended up in an unfamiliar flat.

options.feedback: In needs a container, and a bare table holds nothing inside it.
Under would mean below the table, which is a different position and would be visible only later.
On is correct because leaving an object on a table means resting it on the surface of the table.
During belongs to time and cannot answer where an object was placed.

questions.explanation:
Leaving a small object on a piece of furniture uses on, because the contact with the surface is what matters: on the table.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence with the correct preposition in every gap.
questions.context: A short report about a neighbourhood and its landmarks.

options.text: We arrived on Toledo and stayed in Friday near the cathedral.
options.feedback: On cannot introduce a city name, and in cannot introduce a weekday.

options.text: We arrived at Toledo and stayed on a hotel near the cathedral.
options.feedback: At can introduce a city for some speakers, but a hotel as an enclosed building takes in, not at.

options.text: We arrived in Toledo and stayed at Friday near the cathedral.
options.feedback: In Toledo is right, but a weekday never takes at in this pattern.

options.text: We arrived in Toledo on Friday and stayed in a hotel near the cathedral.
options.feedback: In Toledo for the city, on Friday for the day and in a hotel for an enclosed building are all correct.

questions.explanation:
Cities, hotels and countries take in, while days and dates take on. Each preposition in the correct option matches its own category.

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: He keeps the toolbox ... the bottom shelf.
questions.context: A worker explaining where the toolbox belongs in a garage.

options.feedback: On is correct because a shelf is a surface, and the toolbox rests on that surface.
At would give a vague location without the contact that a shelf provides.
During belongs to a period of time and has no meaning for a physical position.
To marks a destination of movement, while the sentence only states where the toolbox stays.

questions.explanation:
Shelves are surfaces, so objects placed on them take on: on the bottom shelf, on the top of the cupboard.

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: The interview is ... 3 o'clock in the afternoon.
questions.context: A teenager apologising for arriving late to a formal appointment.

options.feedback: In appears with parts of the day such as in the afternoon, but 3 o'clock is a precise moment.
At is correct because an exact hour on the clock is introduced by at.
On marks days and dates, and no day is named in the sentence.
For expresses duration, and the sentence states a moment rather than a length of time.

questions.explanation:
A meeting fixed to an exact hour takes at: at 3 o'clock, at noon. The phrase in the afternoon names a period, not a point.

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: The history books are ... the first corridor, ... the tall shelf.
questions.context: A librarian telling a student where the shelves of a section are.

options.feedback: In the middle of suggests the centre of the space, which the sentence does not state.
On top of needs a surface above something, and no such surface appears in the context.
At the end of the corridor is correct because the end of a corridor is a precise point.
Out of expresses movement from a closed space, which is not what the librarian describes.

questions.explanation:
At the end of marks the limit of a linear space such as a corridor, a queue or a page, and that is where the tall shelf stands.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence where each time and place preposition is used correctly.
questions.context: A correction of a sentence whose prepositions are all wrong.

options.text: We stayed in home during the storm and went out in Sunday morning.
options.feedback: Home is a building word that normally takes at, and Sunday morning takes on, not in.

options.text: We stayed during home the storm and went out on Sunday morning.
options.feedback: During cannot precede home, because home names a place rather than a period.

options.text: We stayed home during the storm and went out at Sunday morning.
options.feedback: At does not introduce a weekday in this pattern, so the last clause fails.

options.text: We stayed at home during the storm and went out on Sunday morning.
options.feedback: At home and during the storm and on Sunday morning each match their own category perfectly.

questions.explanation:
Each preposition belongs to one category: at for points and home, during for a period, on for days. The correct option respects all three.
